newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU/Latin America pledge to forge closer links.
newsitem.headline: EU/Latin America pledge to forge closer links.

text.p: The European Union and Latin America on Tuesday pledged to forge closer relations, aiming for increased trade and planning a first summit before the end of the century.
"Our relations can and will get better," said Dutch foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo following a meeting of 11 Latin American foreign ministers and their 15 EU counterparts.
Van Mierlo said great progress had been made in strengthening trade, political and cultural links and exchanges had developed from "merely reading out statements to having lively exchanges of view".
Officials said a first EU/Latam summit would be held -- probably in the first half of 1998 -- and that either Brazil or Panama were likely venues.

In a move likely to irritate the United States, officials said Cuban leader Fidel Castro would be invited to attend. Washington has made no secret of its desire to see Havana isolated by the international community and last year passed the Helms-Burton Act -- which seeks to quash trade with Cuba -- to much international outrage.

Although ministers did not refer specifically to the act on Tuesday, in a joint statement they condemned "any unilateral measure having extraterritorial effect contrary to international law and to established trade rules".

There was also implied criticism for Washington's policy of "certification", by which the U.S. withdraws trade privileges from countries it believes are not doing enough to combat narcotic drug production.
"Sanctions or certification ... both of these are unilaterism and they are wrong," said Manuel Marin, European Commissioner with responsibility for Latin America.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said responsibility for curbing drug production lay just as much with nations that consumed the final product.
"Drugs are a challenge that we have to deal with together and in solidarity," he said. "Blaming each other doesn't help."
During the meeting the EU approved giving Bolivia 19 million European currency units for a project that will help farmers in the Chamore region convert coca plantations into food farms.

Lucrative generalised system of preferences trade privileges on agricultural and fisheries products were also extended to the five Andean Pact countries -- Venezuela, Colombia, Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru -- to encourage further coca replacement.
In their statement, the ministers also pledged more cooperation on efforts to fight international terrorism.

With the siege of the Japanese embassy in Peru by the radical Tupac Amaru group entering its 113th day on Tuesday, ministers said they "condemned all acts of terrorism, in all its forms and manifestations".
